subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.stage_label: Notice and question — encountering science as a living process
periods.activity_title: What Kind of Questions Do Scientists Ask?
periods.activity_description: Students encounter four surprising answers from science and generate the creative questions that could have produced them. The activity foregrounds the idea that science begins with a question, not an answer, and surfaces students' existing assumptions about what science is.

roles.role_description: Presents the four answers from Activity 1.1 and invites students to generate questions freely, holding back any correction to honour divergent thinking.
Each student independently writes candidate questions for each answer before sharing with the class.
Small groups pool their questions and select the one they find most scientifically interesting to share with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's framing: science is a living process of questioning, not a fixed collection of facts.
Students individually read the four unusual answers and write their own candidate questions for each.
Groups compare questions, notice which are more testable or open-ended, and choose one to present.
Groups share selected questions; class discusses what makes a question 'scientific' — testable, observable, generative.
Teacher closes by naming the chapter's big idea: good scientists are distinguished by the quality of their questions.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the opening unit of the chapter, and its starting point is the inversion Activity 1.1 proposes — presenting answers before questions. A common tendency to watch for is students writing recall questions ('What is this called?') rather than causal or investigable ones; gently redirect by asking 'Could you test that question with an experiment?'. Groups that converge quickly on one question benefit from a prompt such as 'What would happen if the conditions changed?' to deepen divergent thinking.
materials: Printed or board-displayed set of four unusual answers from Activity 1.1

periods.stage_label: Notice and question — encountering science as a living process
periods.activity_title: Science Is Everywhere — A Textbook Tour
periods.activity_description: Students work with the chapter's thematic overview to map the domains previewed — acids and bases, electrical circuits, changes, heat, life processes, motion, light, Earth and Moon — onto a class-made concept web. The activity makes visible how science topics connect across domains rather than sitting in isolation.

roles.role_description: Guides the class through the thematic overview section, pausing at each domain preview to invite brief examples students already know from daily life.
Each group is assigned two or three preview domains and constructs a mini concept-web section showing connections between those domains and an everyday phenomenon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the thematic overview aloud, pausing at each domain so students can name one everyday example they already associate with it.
Groups construct a mini concept-web on paper, linking their assigned domains to each other and to one shared everyday phenomenon from the overview.
Groups briefly present their webs; class notices which domains appear in multiple webs, revealing interconnectedness.
Teacher draws one large connecting web on the board, integrating all groups' contributions to close the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established that science begins with questions; this unit shows the landscape of questions Grade 7 science will explore. Watch for students treating each domain as entirely separate — the chapter explicitly argues for interconnectedness, so probe with 'Which topic on your web touches the one the next group has?'. A good checkpoint before moving on is whether students can articulate one connection between two seemingly different domains using their own words.
materials: Chapter 1 thematic overview section (textbook or printed excerpt)
Large blank paper or chart paper per group

periods.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
periods.activity_title: Ideas That Changed — Reading the Shift
periods.activity_description: Students examine several pairs of 'old idea vs. new understanding' drawn from the chapter's examples — flat Earth, fixed species, spontaneous generation, and similar pivots — and classify each shift by what kind of evidence or question caused the change. They begin building a picture of science as a process that revises itself.

roles.role_description: Presents three or four before-and-after knowledge pairs from the chapter and poses the guiding question: what kind of thing caused each shift?
Groups classify each knowledge shift under a category — new instrument, new observation, new experiment, new question — and justify their classification in one sentence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of knowledge revision by presenting the first before-and-after pair and modelling the classification aloud.
Groups work through the remaining pairs, classifying the type of shift and noting their justification.
Groups share classifications; class discusses cases where groups disagreed and why, revealing that a single shift can be driven by multiple factors.
Teacher consolidates by naming the chapter's key claim: scientific knowledge evolves, and the chapter is asking students to trace how.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from noticing science's breadth (the previous unit) to examining the mechanism of scientific change. A misconception to watch for is the idea that older scientists were simply wrong or foolish — the chapter frames revision as the strength of science, not a failure, so redirect any dismissiveness. Probing question: 'What would it have taken for people at that time to believe the new idea?'
materials: Board or projected list of three to four before-and-after knowledge pairs drawn from chapter content
Classification card templates or notebook columns (label: type of shift | justification)

periods.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
periods.activity_title: The Values That Drive Scientific Change
periods.activity_description: Students identify and name the values that make science capable of revising itself — honesty in recording observations, openness to questioning, and treating science as a collective endeavour — by connecting each value to a concrete example from the chapter's content.

roles.role_description: Introduces the concept of scientific values as the engine of change, using the chapter's framing of scientific temper and collective endeavour, and leads structured discussion.
Each student matches each scientific value named to a concrete example from the chapter or from the concept web built in the previous unit, writing a one-sentence justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the chapter's argument: scientific knowledge changes because scientists hold certain values — honesty, openness, and collectivity — and explains each.
Students individually match each value to a concrete example drawn from the chapter's knowledge-shift pairs and write one-sentence justifications.
Class shares matches; teacher highlights cases where the same example illustrates multiple values simultaneously.
Teacher draws the connection forward: these values are what will be practised across all units in Grade 7, not just discussed in this chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit traced what kind of event caused knowledge to shift; this unit names the values that made those shifts possible. A common conflation to watch for is treating 'honesty' as simply 'not cheating' rather than as recording observations accurately even when they contradict a hypothesis — the chapter's thermometer example is useful here. Checking that students can articulate why collectivity matters (no single person could accumulate all needed evidence alone) signals readiness to move to the next stage.
materials: Board list of three scientific values with brief definitions
Notebooks or worksheets for individual matching activity

periods.stage_label: Explain causally — why science evolves and what sustains that evolution
periods.activity_title: The Engine of Change — Building a Causal Account
periods.activity_description: Students construct a causal explanation for why scientific knowledge changes over time, connecting the values identified in the previous stage to the mechanisms of knowledge revision — new questions, new instruments, collective scrutiny — and producing a written causal chain that could be evaluated.

roles.role_description: Groups draft a written causal chain: 'Scientific knowledge changes because... which is possible because... and is sustained by...' using evidence from the chapter.
Circulates to probe causal links, asking 'What would happen to this chain if the value of honesty were removed?' to stress-test the explanation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the classification and values work from the previous two units and poses the causal question: why does science as a system keep revising itself?
Groups construct their causal chain in writing, grounding each link in a concrete example from the chapter or the classification activity.
Groups read their chains aloud; class identifies which links are well-supported and which need more evidence.
Teacher synthesises across chains, identifying the shared causal logic and naming it as the chapter's central argument.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to move from classifying what changed and naming the values involved, to explaining the causal logic that makes sustained scientific evolution possible — a meaningfully harder operation. Watch for causal chains that list events without linking them ('scientists made new instruments, and then they discovered X') rather than explaining why one made the other possible. The probe question 'What would stop this chain from working?' is effective at revealing whether students have a genuine causal model.
materials: Notebooks or large paper for group causal chains
Board for capturing shared causal elements during synthesis

periods.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
periods.activity_title: Is This Science? Evaluating Real Scenarios
periods.activity_description: Students are given four short scenarios — some depicting genuine scientific practice, others depicting violations of scientific values or processes — and must classify each as 'science', 'not science', or 'science done poorly', providing a causal justification that references the values and processes identified across the chapter.

roles.role_description: Each student reads the four scenarios and independently classifies each with a written justification before group discussion.
Groups compare individual classifications, negotiate disagreements using the chapter's framework of values and processes, and produce a consensus justification.
Facilitates whole-class debrief, probing cases of genuine disagreement and connecting them to the chapter's argument about science as a collective and self-correcting endeavour.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the four scenarios and explains the classification task: students must justify using the chapter's framework, not intuition alone.
Students individually classify each scenario and write a one-sentence justification.
Groups compare, negotiate, and produce a consensus classification and justification for each scenario.
Whole-class debrief focuses on the two or three scenarios that generated most disagreement, with the teacher pressing for causal justification.
Teacher notes which scenarios were hardest to classify and frames this as evidence that the boundary of 'science' is itself something science keeps examining.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit built a causal account of why science evolves; this unit asks students to apply that account to evaluate unfamiliar scenarios — the highest-order operation before the synthesis. A common error is classifying by topic ('this is about nature, so it must be science') rather than by process and values; redirect by asking 'Which values from our framework does this person's behaviour reflect?'. Students who can articulate why 'science done poorly' is still classifiable as science have grasped the chapter's nuanced argument.
materials: Four printed or board-displayed short scenarios (teacher-authored, grounded in the chapter's examples of scientific values and processes)
homework: Choose one scientific discovery you have heard of outside school and write three sentences explaining what kind of change it represented — new instrument, new question, or new collective scrutiny — using the classification framework from this unit.

periods.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
periods.activity_title: The Ever-Evolving Story — A Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.activity_description: Students construct and defend a personal statement on what makes science 'ever-evolving', drawing on the chapter's full argument: science changes through questioning, evidence, collective scrutiny, and values such as honesty and openness. The activity requires integrating the chapter's epistemological claims into a coherent position that could withstand peer challenge.

roles.role_description: Each student drafts a short written statement (three to four sentences) defending a position on what makes scientific knowledge capable of evolving over time.
Groups read each other's statements and pose one challenge question per statement; the author must respond using the chapter's framework of values and processes.
Facilitates the challenge round and closes by articulating the chapter's core insight: science is not a set of facts but a collective, value-driven human endeavour that sustains its own revision.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the synthesis task: students have worked through questioning, classifying knowledge shifts, naming values, building causal accounts, and evaluating scenarios — now they must integrate these into a single position.
Students individually draft their three-to-four sentence statements, drawing on any concept, example, or argument from the chapter.
Groups exchange statements and each member poses one challenge question; the author responds orally using the chapter's framework.
Two or three particularly sharp exchanges are shared with the class; the teacher names what made each response strong or incomplete.
Teacher delivers a closing statement restating the chapter's title claim and connecting it to the inquiry journey that will continue across the rest of Grade 7.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws the entire chapter together and must stand alone — it assumes the chapter's content is known but not any particular earlier activity. The key quality marker is whether students' statements are argued rather than listed: a statement that says 'science evolves because of new questions, honesty, and collective work' is a list; one that explains why each element is necessary and how they interact is an argument. Watch for students who can challenge but cannot defend — they have the critical capacity but need support constructing a positive position.
materials: Notebooks or paper for individual statements
No additional materials required — this unit works from the chapter's ideas alone

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Notice and question — encountering science as a living process
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students generate scientific questions from unusual answers and map the interconnected domains of science previewed in the chapter, surfacing the idea that science is a living process of questioning rather than a fixed body of facts.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can generate testable or open-ended questions from a given phenomenon and articulate at least one connection between two science domains, demonstrating that science begins with questioning rather than with answers.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify historical knowledge shifts by the type of event that caused them and identify the scientific values — honesty, openness, collectivity — that make such shifts possible, connecting each value to a concrete example.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a scientific knowledge shift by the type of evidence or process that drove it and match each scientific value to a concrete example from the chapter, showing that knowledge revision depends on both mechanism and value.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causally — why science evolves and what sustains that evolution
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a written causal chain explaining why scientific knowledge continues to evolve, linking values to mechanisms and grounding each link in a concrete example from the chapter.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can produce a written causal explanation of why scientific knowledge evolves that connects at least two values to at least two mechanisms of change, with each causal link explicitly justified rather than merely asserted.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students evaluate unfamiliar scenarios against the chapter's framework of values and processes, classify them with justified reasoning, and synthesise the chapter's argument into a personal written position that can withstand peer challenge.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate whether a described practice constitutes scientific inquiry by applying the chapter's framework of values and processes, and can defend a coherent written position on what makes scientific knowledge capable of evolving over time.

assessment_items.stage_label: Notice and question — encountering science as a living process
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can generate testable or open-ended questions from a given phenomenon and articulate at least one connection between two science domains, demonstrating that science begins with questioning rather than with answers.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is given this unusual answer: 'Because no one had ever asked that question before.' Which of the following questions most likely produced this answer in a scientific context?

options.label: A
options.text: Why do birds migrate south in winter?

options.label: B
options.text: What is the boiling point of water?

options.label: C
options.text: Why does the Earth orbit the Sun and not the other way around?

options.label: D
options.text: How many planets are in the Solar System?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student associates scientific questions with observable natural phenomena but selects a familiar recall question rather than one that challenged an entrenched assumption — shows limited grasp of the chapter's point about paradigm-shifting questions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student selects a well-defined measurement question; this reflects a misconception that any question with a numerical answer is a deeper scientific question, rather than recognising that the answer 'no one had ever asked' signals a question that broke convention.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses a factual inventory question with a question that shifted thinking; this reflects recall of science content rather than engagement with the chapter's argument about what makes a question scientifically generative.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with abstract framing may be supported by being asked to restate the answer in their own words before choosing a question. Students who finish quickly can be asked to generate a second question that would also produce the given answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Notice and question — encountering science as a living process
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can generate testable or open-ended questions from a given phenomenon and articulate at least one connection between two science domains, demonstrating that science begins with questioning rather than with answers.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes science as a 'living process' rather than a collection of facts. Which of the following best illustrates this idea?

options.label: A
options.text: A student memorises the periodic table to score well on a test.

options.label: B
options.text: A teacher writes the boiling point of water on the board and students copy it.

options.label: C
options.text: A student notices that ice melts faster in sunlight and wonders what other factors speed up melting.

options.label: D
options.text: A student reads that sound travels faster in solids than in gases and underlines it.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student associates science with school performance rather than inquiry; indicates the misconception that science is primarily a body of content to be absorbed rather than a process of questioning.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses transmission of known facts with the process of science; shows the chapter's target misconception that science is defined by facts rather than by the act of questioning and investigating.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student recognises that reading about science is related to science but does not distinguish passive reception from active inquiry — a partial understanding that the chapter directly addresses.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are less confident in reading can be asked to act out each option briefly before choosing; students with strong language skills can be asked to rewrite their chosen option to make it an even clearer example of science as a living process.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a scientific knowledge shift by the type of evidence or process that drove it and match each scientific value to a concrete example from the chapter, showing that knowledge revision depends on both mechanism and value.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: For centuries, people believed that the Earth was flat. When sailors and astronomers accumulated observations from many different places and times showing the Earth was spherical, the old idea was revised. What type of shift caused this change in scientific knowledge?

options.label: A
options.text: A single scientist proved the old idea wrong in one experiment.

options.label: B
options.text: A new instrument was invented that made the old idea irrelevant.

options.label: C
options.text: Collective observations from multiple sources accumulated until the evidence could no longer be ignored.

options.label: D
options.text: A government authority declared the old idea incorrect and replaced it.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student holds the misconception that scientific breakthroughs are always the work of a lone genius proving others wrong — the chapter specifically argues against this by framing science as a collective endeavour.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student over-applies the 'new instrument' category from the classification activity, confusing technological change with the accumulation of distributed observational evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates authority with scientific evidence — a significant conceptual error that the chapter's framing of scientific values (questioning over deference) directly addresses.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the historical context unfamiliar can be asked to describe what they already know about how we know the Earth is spherical; students who are confident can be asked to name a second historical example that fits the same category.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a scientific knowledge shift by the type of evidence or process that drove it and match each scientific value to a concrete example from the chapter, showing that knowledge revision depends on both mechanism and value.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: During a science experiment, a student measures the temperature at which water boils and gets a reading of 98°C instead of the expected 100°C. The student records 98°C accurately in the notebook. Which scientific value does this action best demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Collectivity — the student is sharing findings with the group.

options.label: B
options.text: Openness — the student is willing to try a different experiment.

options.label: C
options.text: Honesty — the student records the actual observation even when it differs from the expected value.

options.label: D
options.text: Curiosity — the student is interested in finding out why the reading is unexpected.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates the act of recording with sharing — a confusion between the value of honesty (in data recording) and collectivity (in knowledge building), both of which appear in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses openness-to-revision with willingness to change procedure, a related but distinct concept — indicates partial engagement with the chapter's value taxonomy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student identifies the emotional state (curiosity) that might follow the unexpected result rather than the value enacted in the moment of recording — shows confusion between scientific disposition and scientific value as the chapter defines it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to distinguish the values can be asked to role-play what each option would look like as a physical action; students who grasp the distinction quickly can be asked to describe a situation where all three values are demonstrated simultaneously.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace and classify — how scientific knowledge changes over time
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a scientific knowledge shift by the type of evidence or process that drove it and match each scientific value to a concrete example from the chapter, showing that knowledge revision depends on both mechanism and value.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: The idea that life could arise spontaneously from non-living matter (for example, that mice could emerge from grain) was once widely believed. It was eventually revised through a series of carefully designed experiments by multiple scientists over time. Name the type of shift that caused this change and identify one scientific value that made the revision possible. Explain your answer in two to three sentences.
expected_elements: Identifies the shift as driven by new experimental evidence (or: systematic experimentation as a mechanism of change).
Names at least one scientific value — honesty, openness, or collectivity — and links it to the revision process.
Provides a one-sentence explanation of why that value was necessary for the shift to occur.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find written responses challenging can first draw or narrate the shift as a before-and-after diagram and then annotate which value appears at which step. Students who are fluent writers can be asked to explain why the shift would have been impossible without that value.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causally — why science evolves and what sustains that evolution
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can produce a written causal explanation of why scientific knowledge evolves that connects at least two values to at least two mechanisms of change, with each causal link explicitly justified rather than merely asserted.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A student argues: 'Science keeps changing because scientists keep asking new questions.' A classmate responds: 'But asking questions alone is not enough — the questions have to be shared and tested by others too.' Which of the following best explains why the classmate's response strengthens the original claim?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that asking questions is unnecessary if experiments are done correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: It adds the mechanism of collective scrutiny, showing that change requires both questioning and shared testing — not questioning alone.

options.label: C
options.text: It proves that the original student was wrong about questions being important.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that only professional scientists can cause scientific knowledge to change.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student misreads the classmate's response as a rejection of questioning — this is a comprehension-level error that reveals the student has not yet grasped the additive (not oppositional) logic of the causal chain.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student interprets the classmate as contradicting the original claim rather than extending it — shows failure to track causal chain logic, treating scientific argument as debate rather than collaborative refinement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces the misconception that expertise is the gatekeeping mechanism for scientific change — this directly contradicts the chapter's argument about science as a collective human endeavour open to anyone who follows its values and processes.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract dialogue format can be asked to rewrite the exchange as a simple if-then statement before choosing. Students who are confident can be asked to add a third step to the causal chain that both students have left out.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causally — why science evolves and what sustains that evolution
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can produce a written causal explanation of why scientific knowledge evolves that connects at least two values to at least two mechanisms of change, with each causal link explicitly justified rather than merely asserted.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: If the value of honesty were removed from scientific practice, which of the following would most directly break down in the process by which scientific knowledge evolves?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists would stop being curious about new phenomena.

options.label: B
options.text: Observations would be reported inaccurately, making collective scrutiny of evidence impossible.

options.label: C
options.text: New scientific instruments would no longer be invented.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists from different countries would stop collaborating.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates the value of honesty with the disposition of curiosity — shows that the student has not yet separated the values taxonomy from the broader scientific attitudes the chapter describes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student associates honesty with technological development rather than with data recording and evidence sharing — a category error that shows the student has not yet traced the causal role of honesty in the knowledge-revision process.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses honesty with the broader value of collectivity or international cooperation — indicates the student has not yet differentiated among the three values the chapter identifies and linked each to its specific causal function.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the counterfactual ('if honesty were removed') abstract can be given a concrete scenario: 'A scientist gets an unexpected result and writes down the expected result instead — what happens next?' Students who answer quickly can be asked to explain which step in the causal chain is most vulnerable to dishonesty.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causally — why science evolves and what sustains that evolution
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can produce a written causal explanation of why scientific knowledge evolves that connects at least two values to at least two mechanisms of change, with each causal link explicitly justified rather than merely asserted.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Scientific knowledge changes just because scientists discover new things.' Write a two-to-three sentence response that improves this explanation by adding at least one value and one mechanism that together make change possible. Justify each addition.
expected_elements: Identifies at least one scientific value (honesty, openness, or collectivity) and states why it is necessary for change to occur.
Identifies at least one mechanism of change (new question, new instrument, collective scrutiny, experimental testing) and links it causally to the value named.
Shows that the original explanation is incomplete rather than simply wrong — the revision adds to it rather than replacing it.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to begin can be given a sentence starter: 'It is true that new discoveries drive change, but this is only possible because...' Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to identify what would happen to their causal chain if the mechanism they named were blocked.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate whether a described practice constitutes scientific inquiry by applying the chapter's framework of values and processes, and can defend a coherent written position on what makes scientific knowledge capable of evolving over time.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A researcher observes results that contradict their existing theory. Instead of publishing these results, they discard them and report only the findings that support their theory. Using the chapter's framework, which of the following best evaluates this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: This is acceptable science because the researcher still used experiments to collect data.

options.label: B
options.text: This is not science because the researcher did not use a laboratory.

options.label: C
options.text: This is science done poorly because the process of inquiry was followed but the value of honesty was violated, making collective scrutiny of the real evidence impossible.

options.label: D
options.text: This is not science because the researcher already had a theory before observing.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student evaluates by procedure alone (was data collected?) without applying the values framework — shows that the student has classified the process as scientific but has not yet integrated values as a necessary component of evaluation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student applies a setting-based criterion (laboratory) rather than a values-and-process criterion — a misconception the chapter directly addresses when it notes that science can be done in any setting, not just formal laboratories.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student applies the misconception that having a prior theory disqualifies the work as science — this inverts the chapter's argument, which describes hypothesis-formation (having a theory) as a normal and necessary part of scientific inquiry.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to use the three-category classification from the scenario activity (science / not science / science done poorly) as a scaffold before choosing. Students who are confident can be asked to explain what the researcher could have done differently at each step to restore both the process and the value.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate whether a described practice constitutes scientific inquiry by applying the chapter's framework of values and processes, and can defend a coherent written position on what makes scientific knowledge capable of evolving over time.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: Two students debate the following claim: 'Science will eventually reach a final, complete answer to every question.' Using the chapter's argument about how scientific knowledge evolves, which evaluation of this claim is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct because science gets more accurate over time and will eventually be complete.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is incorrect because scientists are not smart enough to answer all questions.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is unlikely because the chapter shows that each new answer generates new questions, making science an open-ended and self-revising process.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is correct because new instruments will eventually make every question answerable.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student accepts a linear-progress model of science (more accurate → eventually complete) that the chapter explicitly challenges by showing that revision is perpetual rather than convergent toward closure.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student attributes the open-endedness of science to human limitation rather than to the generative structure of inquiry — a misconception that misses the chapter's argument that new questions arise from new answers regardless of the intelligence of the scientists.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student over-applies the 'new instrument' mechanism from the classification stage, conflating the expansion of observational capacity with the closure of questioning — shows incomplete integration of the chapter's causal argument.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the philosophical claim abstract can be grounded by asking them to recall one example from the chapter where a solved question generated a new question. Students who are confident can be asked to construct a hypothetical counter-argument and then explain why the chapter's framework would refute it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and evaluate — science as a collective human endeavour with values and limits
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate whether a described practice constitutes scientific inquiry by applying the chapter's framework of values and processes, and can defend a coherent written position on what makes scientific knowledge capable of evolving over time.

competency.competency_text: Identifies how scientific knowledge and ideas have changed over time and recognises the scientific values inherent across the evolution of scientific knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A student makes the following argument: 'Science is ever-evolving because scientists never stop being curious.' Evaluate this argument. In your response, explain what is correct about it, what it leaves out, and how it should be extended to give a more complete account of why scientific knowledge keeps changing. Write four to five sentences.
look_for: Identifies what is correct in the original argument — curiosity or the disposition to keep questioning is a genuine driver of scientific inquiry.

Identifies a significant gap — curiosity alone does not explain the mechanism of revision; the response must add at least one mechanism (collective scrutiny, experimental testing, new instruments, or new questions built on old answers).

Identifies a second gap — the argument does not account for the values that make sustained inquiry possible (honesty, openness, collectivity); at least one value must be named and its causal role explained.
Produces an extended version of the argument that integrates curiosity, at least one mechanism, and at least one value into a coherent causal account.
The evaluative move is explicit — the student does not simply add information but explains why the additions change the quality of the explanation.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to begin can be given a three-part structure: 'The argument is correct that... However, it leaves out... A more complete account would say...' Students who are fluent can be asked to generate a further counter-argument against their extended account and evaluate it.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Practice | Values present? (Yes/No) | Mechanism of change present? (Yes/No) | Classification (Science / Not Science / Science Done Poorly) | Justification
A group of farmers notices that their crop yield drops every third year and begins recording rainfall, soil type, and yield data across several seasons, sharing findings with neighbouring villages. | | | |
A scientist gets unexpected results from an experiment, suspects a mistake, and quietly adjusts the numbers in the data to match the expected outcome before publishing. | | | |

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each practice described: (1) identify whether scientific values are present, (2) identify whether a mechanism of change is present, (3) classify the practice as Science, Not Science, or Science Done Poorly, and (4) write one sentence justifying your classification using the chapter's framework of values and processes.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the chapter's three scientific values (honesty, openness, collectivity) and four mechanisms of change (new question, new instrument, collective scrutiny, experimental testing) as your framework. A practice can be classified as Science Done Poorly if the process is present but a value is violated. Your justification must name at least one value or mechanism.
format_of_output: Completed table with all cells filled
One-sentence justification per row naming at least one value or mechanism from the chapter's framework

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to evaluate practices against the chapter's framework and produce a justified classification — a sorting task with written justification is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates the student's capacity to simultaneously apply the chapter's values framework and mechanisms taxonomy to evaluate unfamiliar practices, producing a justified position rather than an intuitive label — the cognitive operation of evaluation as the chapter defines it.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table's two binary columns (values present? / mechanism present?) are diagnostic: a student who can fill these in accurately but struggles with the classification column has the components but not the integrating logic. A student who classifies correctly but writes a weak justification has the evaluative intuition but not the causal articulation. The most significant responses will show that 'Science Done Poorly' (Row 2) is the hardest category because it requires holding both 'process followed' and 'value violated' simultaneously. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Science open task menu — a predict-and-explain task or a procedure evaluation task would also serve this LO.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly classify all four rows with justifications that name a specific value or mechanism and explain its causal role; treat 'Science Done Poorly' as distinct from 'Not Science' and articulate why. Weak responses: classify by topic or surface familiarity rather than by framework; write justifications that restate the scenario rather than apply the framework; conflate 'Not Science' and 'Science Done Poorly' by treating any value violation as a disqualification from being science at all.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the four-row table overwhelming can be asked to complete two rows (Rows 1 and 2 are the most contrasting pair) and then explain their choices orally. Students who complete all rows quickly can be asked to design a fifth scenario that would produce genuine disagreement about classification and explain why it is hard to classify.
